interactions: Pyridostigmine + lisinopril: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction; monitor blood pressure as acetylcholinesterase inhibition may cause mild bradycardia
Statins (atorvastatin): rare case reports of statin-associated inflammatory myopathy that may mimic or worsen neuromuscular fatigue; CK monitoring appropriate in context of concurrent NMJ disease

Aminoglycosides (e.g., gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin): MAJOR — impair presynaptic calcium-mediated ACh release, precipitate myasthenic crisis; contraindicated or use only with extreme caution in MG
Fluoroquinolones (e.g., ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): MAJOR — FDA black-box warning; exacerbate MG via NMJ blockade
Telithromycin: CONTRAINDICATED in MG — blocks NMJ transmission; associated with respiratory failure and deaths in MG patients
IV magnesium sulfate: MAJOR — blocks presynaptic ACh release and postsynaptic receptor; can precipitate myasthenic crisis; avoid unless no alternative (e.g., eclampsia, refractory hypomagnesemia)

Non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers (vecuronium, rocuronium, atracurium): MAJOR — markedly enhanced and prolonged effect in MG; if anaesthesia required, dose at 10-20% of standard; avoid without MG-experienced anaesthesiology

Procainamide: MAJOR — antiarrhythmic with NMJ-blocking properties; avoid in MG

key_clinical_evidence: Double-seronegativity (AChR-negative AND MuSK-negative) does NOT exclude myasthenia gravis — a subset of 10-15% of generalized MG patients are seronegative on conventional assays, and LRP4 antibodies account for approximately 1-5% of double-seronegative cases.

Single-fiber EMG is the gold-standard test with sensitivity exceeding 95% in generalized MG, including seronegative subtypes; abnormal jitter and blocking are objective markers of NMJ dysfunction independent of antibody status.

Normal or borderline RNS (below the 10% decrement threshold) is well described in seronegative MG and in LRP4-MG specifically — a non-diagnostic RNS increases the diagnostic weight of SFEMG rather than excluding the diagnosis.

LRP4 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4) is a co-receptor for agrin and part of the agrin-LRP4-MuSK signalling complex critical for NMJ formation and maintenance; LRP4 antibodies disrupt this complex and cause MG without AChR or MuSK antibodies.

The functional disorder misattribution trap is the dominant red herring: prior clinicians interpreted double-seronegativity and normal RNS as excluding MG, anchoring on a functional label; fatigable diurnal ptosis and objective SFEMG abnormalities are organic markers that override this anchoring.
CT chest with contrast is required for thymoma screening in all confirmed MG — including seronegative and LRP4-positive cases — regardless of antibody subtype.

A positive ice-pack test (ptosis improves >2 mm on cooling) is a rapid bedside confirmatory test with approximately 80% sensitivity for ocular MG; it supports NMJ localisation before the SFEMG result is available.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 48-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, and obstructive sleep apnoea presented to the neurology inpatient service for evaluation of progressive, fluctuating left ptosis and diplopia over 4 months. He initially noticed intermittent left eyelid drooping when driving home after long shifts, which he attributed to fatigue from work and disrupted sleep. His wife noted that the drooping was consistently worse in the evening and absent in the morning. Over the following 6 weeks, he developed horizontal diplopia during sustained lateral gaze, and mild difficulty chewing through a full meal without jaw fatigue. He also began experiencing slurred speech after prolonged speaking — specifically after more than 30-40 minutes of telephone calls. His primary care physician initially attributed symptoms to work-related stress and referred him for sleep optimisation and CPAP pressure adjustment. Repeat overnight oximetry showed adequate CPAP compliance (AHI <5). His symptoms did not improve. He was then evaluated by ophthalmology, who found no structural orbital pathology and measured intraocular pressure as normal; they noted the left ptosis was variable across the visit and referred to neurology.

At a neurology outpatient visit two months prior to this admission, AChR binding and blocking antibodies were checked and returned negative; MuSK antibodies were checked 3 weeks later at an outside laboratory and also returned negative. The treating neurologist interpreted the double-negative result as 'essentially excluding myasthenia gravis' and attributed his symptoms to a functional/psychogenic overlay in the context of occupational stress. The patient was referred to psychology. He completed 6 weeks of CBT-based sessions without benefit and was subsequently admitted for inpatient evaluation after his wife witnessed visible ptosis and slurred speech at dinner and called the neurology team.

He denied any limb weakness at rest, sensory disturbance, headache, weight loss, night sweats, cough, or haemoptysis. He denied use of aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, or any new medications. His symptoms are consistently worse later in the day and dramatically improved after one hour of rest, which he initially attributed to recovering from fatigue. He has no history of thyroid disease.
